newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sweden seen waiting with EMU despite Riksbank view.
newsitem.headline: Sweden seen waiting with EMU despite Riksbank view.

text.p: Sweden is likely to adopt a wait-and-see stance on European monetary union, reflecting scepticism among the public and politicians, rather than accepting the central bank's advice to join a single currency early on, economists say.

Swedish membership of economic and monetary union (EMU) from the start in 1999 "is not totally ruled out even if the probability is relatively low," said economist Ake Gustafsson at Swedbank in Stockholm.
Gustafsson and other economists believe Sweden will not take part in EMU's launch but leave the door open for possible membership a few years later.
"I believe (the government) will want to try and keep it open to join in the second wave," said Carl Hamilton, chief economist at Handelsbanken.

Last week, Prime Minister Goran Persson repeated that the decision on whether to join EMU was "still an open question" even though Sweden would meet the Maastricht treaty's economic criteria for qualifying for the single currency.

His Social Democrats are due to decide their position at a party congress in September and parliament will make the final decision in October or November -- just a few months before EU leaders are due to rule on which countries can join.
Persson stressed that a decision on EMU must be anchored in Swedish society.
"If I should judge now from the Swedish opinion, it's a negative decision. But you don't know. Much can happen and it is still an open question," he said on a visit to Luxembourg.

He has called for a wide public debate on membership but the cabinet has cooled considerably because of opinion polls showing strong public distaste for monetary union. Over the last few weeks, ministers have expressed differing views on the benefits of EMU.
As the first major public institution to comment, the powerful Riksbank last Friday said Sweden should be among the first wave to join in January 1999.
The Riksbank said it rejected the conclusions of an official inquiry into Swedish EMU membership, saying the report had underestimated the benefits to the country.
"Our possibility to have an impact on the development of the Union would be less if we stayed outside," Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom said.

The Riksbank said the inquiry report by Professor Lars Calmfors published last year was overcautious. It concluded the risks of EMU membership were severe and that Sweden should not be among the first nations to join.

Handelsbanken's Hamilton said the Riksbank statement was a "fairly scathing criticism" of the Calmfors report and this would diminish its value as a basis for decision. "But I don't think this will really influence the government's decision about not joining in the first wave in 1999," he said.
Hamilton said, however, that the clear position of the Riksbank increased the chances of Sweden joining in a second wave in 2001 and also paved the way for a more open and sound debate about EMU.

Hamilton, advocating early membership, said it was important to be in EMU from the start, partly as it was then that it would be decided how the future European Central Bank would operate its monetary policy.
"I don't think the arguments that we must stay out because of employment reasons are well founded," he added.
